entries.b50b79f792dec9c74ef16caf2d44747cd87cda89: <div sID="gen10039" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="32" osisID="Job.32" sID="Job.32"/> <div eID="gen10039" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10040" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10041" type="x-p"/> The stage is clear, for Job and his three friends have sat down, and neither he nor they have any thing more to say; it is therefore very seasonable for a moderator to interpose, and Elihu is the man. In this chapter we have, I. Some account of him, his parentage, his presence at this dispute, and his sentiments concerning it, <reference osisRef="Job.32.1-Job.32.5">ver. 1-5</reference>. II. The apology he made for his bold undertaking to speak to a question which had been so largely and learnedly argued by his seniors. He pleads, 1. That, though he had not the experience of an old man, yet he had the understanding of a man, <reference osisRef="Job.32.6-Job.32.10">ver. 6-10</reference>. 2. That he had patiently heard all they had to say, <reference osisRef="Job.32.11-Job.32.13">ver. 11-13</reference>. 3. That he had something new to offer, <reference osisRef="Job.32.14-Job.32.17">ver. 14-17</reference>. 4. That his mind was full of this matter, and it would be a refreshment to him to give it vent, <reference osisRef="Job.32.18-Job.32.20">ver. 18-20</reference>. 5. That he was resolved to speak impartially, <reference osisRef="Job.32.21-Job.32.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>. And he did speak so well to this matter that Job made no reply to him, and God gave him no rebuke when he checked both Job himself and his other three friends.
entries.5f187cc50109f1facf0f6aa977c9c54a9eaf2090: <div eID="gen10041" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10040" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Elihu. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10042" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he <hi type="italic">was</hi> righteous in his own eyes. <hi type="super">2</hi> Then was kindled the wrath of Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself rather than God. <hi type="super">3</hi> Also against his three friends was his wrath kindled, because they had found no answer, and <hi type="italic">yet</hi> had condemned <reference osisRef="Job.4">Job. 4</reference> Now Elihu had waited till Job had spoken, because they <hi type="italic">were</hi> elder than he. <hi type="super">5</hi> When Elihu saw that <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no answer in the mouth of <hi type="italic">these</hi> three men, then his wrath was kindled. <div eID="gen10042" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10043" type="x-p"/> Usually young men are the disputants and old men the moderators; but here, when old men were the disputants, as a rebuke to them for their unbecoming heat, a young man is raised up to be the moderator. Divers of Job's friends were present, that came to visit him and to receive instruction. Now here we have, <div eID="gen10043" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10044" type="x-p"/> I. The reason why his three friends were now silent. They <hi type="italic">ceased to answer him,</hi> and let him have his saying, <hi type="italic">because he was righteous in his own eyes.</hi> This was the reason they gave why they said no more, because it was to no purpose to argue with a man that was so opinionative, <reference osisRef="Job.32.1">v. 1</reference>. Those that are self-conceited are indeed hard to be wrought upon; there is more hope of a fool (a fool of God's making) than of those who are fools of their own making, <reference osisRef="Prov.26.12">Prov. xxvi. 12</reference>. But they did not judge fairly concerning Job: he was really righteous before God, and not righteous in his own eyes only; so that it was only to save their own credit that they made this the reason of their silence, as peevish disputants commonly do when they find themselves run a-ground and are not willing to own themselves unable to make their part good. <div eID="gen10044" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10045" type="x-p"/> II. The reasons why Elihu, the fourth, now spoke. His name <hi type="italic">Elihu</hi> signifies <hi type="italic">My God is he.</hi> They had all tried in vain to convince Job, but <hi type="italic">my God is he</hi> that can and will do it, and did it at last: he only can open the understanding. He is said to be a <hi type="italic">Buzite,</hi> from Buz, Nahor's second son (<reference osisRef="Gen.22.21">Gen. xxii. 21</reference>), and <hi type="italic">of the kindred of Ram,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">Aram</hi> (so some), whence the Syrians or Aramites descended and were denominated, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.21">Gen. xxii. 21</reference>. <hi type="italic">Of the kindred of Abram;</hi> so the Chaldee-paraphrase, supposing him to be first called <hi type="italic">Ram—high,</hi> then <hi type="italic">Abram—a high father,</hi> and lastly <hi type="italic">Abraham—the high father of a multitude.</hi> Elihu was not so well known as the rest, and therefore is more particularly described thus. <div eID="gen10045" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10046" type="x-p"/> 1. Elihu spoke because he was angry and thought he had good cause to be so. When he had made his observations upon the dispute he did not go away and calumniate the disputants, striking them secretly with a malicious censorious tongue, but what he had to say he would say before their faces, that they might vindicate themselves if they could. (1.) He was angry at Job, because he thought he did not speak so reverently of God as he ought to have done; and that was too true (<reference osisRef="Job.32.2">v. 2</reference>): <hi type="italic">He justified himself more than God,</hi> that is, took more care and pains to clear himself from the imputation of unrighteousness in being thus afflicted than to clear God from the imputation of unrighteousness in afflicting him, as if he were more concerned for his own honour than for God's; whereas he should, in the first place, have justified God and cleared his glory, and then he might well enough have left his own reputation to shift for itself. Note, A gracious heart is jealous for the honour of God, and cannot but be angry when that is neglected or postponed, or when any injury is done it. Nor is it any breach of the law of meekness to be angry at our friends when they are offensive to God. <hi type="italic">Get thee behind me, Satan,</hi> says Christ to Simon. Elihu owned Job to be a good man, and yet would not say as he said when he thought he said amiss: it is too great a compliment to our friends not to tell them of their faults. (2.) He was angry at his friends because he thought they had not conducted themselves so charitably towards Job as they ought to have done (<reference osisRef="Job.32.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">They had found no answer, and yet had condemned Job.</hi> They had adjudged him to be a hypocrite, a wicked man, and would not recede from that sentence concerning him; and yet they could not prove him so, nor disprove the evidences he produced of his integrity. They could not make good the premises, and yet held fast the conclusion. They had no reply to make to his arguments, and yet they would not yield, but, right or wrong, would run him down; and this was not fair. Seldom is a quarrel begun, and more seldom is a quarrel carried on to the length that this was, in which there is not a fault on both sides. Elihu, as became a moderator, took part with neither, but was equally displeased with the mistakes and mismanagement of both. Those that in good earnest seek for truth must thus be impartial in their judgments concerning the contenders, and not reject what is true and good on either side for the sake of what is amiss, nor approve or defend what is amiss for the sake of what is true and good, but must learn to separate between the precious and the vile. <div eID="gen10046" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10047" type="x-p"/> 2. Elihu spoke because he thought that it was time to speak, and that now, at length, it had come to his turn, <reference osisRef="Job.32.4-Job.32.5">v. 4, 5</reference>. (1.) He had waited on Job's speeches, had patiently heard him out, until the words of Job were ended. (2.) He had waited on his friends' silence, so that, as he would not interrupt him, so he would not prevent them, not because they were wiser than he, but because they were older than he, and therefore it was expected by the company that they should speak first; and Elihu was very modest, and would by no means offer to abridge them of their privilege. Some certain rules of precedency must be observed, for the keeping of order. Though inward real honour will attend true wisdom and worth, yet, since every man will think himself or his friend the wisest and worthiest, this can afford no certain rule for the outward ceremonial honour, which therefore must attend seniority either of age or office; and this respect the seniors may the better require because they paid it when they were juniors, and the juniors may the better pay because they shall have it when they come to be seniors.
entries.d9dd9b686d2e3afdf92c83f424b5d2817ff7d28c: <div eID="gen10047" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10048" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite answered and said, I <hi type="italic">am</hi> young, and ye <hi type="italic">are</hi> very old; wherefore I was afraid, and durst not show you mine opinion. <hi type="super">7</hi> I said, Days should speak, and multitude of years should teach wisdom. <hi type="super">8</hi> But <hi type="italic">there is</hi> a spirit in man: and the inspiration of the Almighty giveth them understanding. <hi type="super">9</hi> Great men are not <hi type="italic">always</hi> wise: neither do the aged understand judgment. <hi type="super">10</hi> Therefore I said, Hearken to me; I also will show mine opinion. <hi type="super">11</hi> Behold, I waited for your words; I gave ear to your reasons, whilst ye searched out what to say. <hi type="super">12</hi> Yea, I attended unto you, and, behold, <hi type="italic">there was</hi> none of you that convinced Job, <hi type="italic">or</hi> that answered his words: <hi type="super">13</hi> Lest ye should say, We have found out wisdom: God thrusteth him down, not man. <hi type="super">14</hi> Now he hath not directed <hi type="italic">his</hi> words against me: neither will I answer him with your speeches. <div eID="gen10048" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> Elihu here appears to have been, <div eID="gen10049" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10050" type="x-p"/> I. A man of great modesty and humility. Though a young man, and a man of abilities, yet not pert, and confident, and assuming: his face shone, and, like Moses, he did not know it, which made it shine so much the brighter. Let it be observed by all, especially by young people, as worthy their imitation, 1. What a diffidence he had of himself and of his own judgment (<reference osisRef="Job.32.6">v. 6</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I am young, and therefore I was afraid, and durst not show you my opinion,</hi> for fear I should either prove mistaken or do that which was unbecoming me." He was so observant of all that passed, and applied his mind so closely to what he heard, that he had formed in himself a judgment of it. He neither neglected it as foreign, nor declined it as intricate; but, how clear soever the matter was to himself, he was afraid to deliver his mind upon it, because he differed in his sentiments from those that were older than he. Note, It becomes us to be suspicious of our own judgment in matters of doubtful disputation, to be swift to hear the sentiments of others and slow to speak our own, especially when we go contrary to the judgment of those for whom, upon the score of their learning and piety, we justly have a veneration. 2. What a deference he paid to his seniors, and what great expectations he had from them, (<reference osisRef="Job.32.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I said, Days should speak.</hi> Note, Age and experience give a man great advantage in judging of things, both as they furnish a man with so much the more matter for his thoughts to work upon and as they ripen and improve the facilities he is to work with, which is a good reason why old people should take pains both to learn themselves and to teach others (else the advantages of their age are a reproach to them), and why young people should attend on their instructions. It is a good <hi type="italic">lodging with an old disciple,</hi> <reference osisRef="Acts.21.16">Acts xxi. 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.4">Tit. ii. 4</reference>. Elihu's modesty appeared in the patient attention he gave to what his seniors said, <reference osisRef="Job.32.11-Job.32.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. He waited for their words as one that expected much from them, agreeably to the opinion he had of these grave men. He gave ear to their reasons, that he might take their meaning, and fully understand what was the drift of their discourse and what the force of their arguments. He attended to them with diligence and care, and this, (1.) Though they were slow, and took up a great deal of time in searching out what to say. Though they had often to seek for matter and words, paused and hesitated, and were unready at their work, yet he overlooked that, and <hi type="italic">gave ear to their reasons,</hi> which, if really convincing, he would not think the less so for the disadvantages of the delivery of them. (2.) Though they trifled and made nothing of it, though none of them answered Job's words nor said what was proper to convince him, yet he attended to them, in hopes they would bring it to some head at last. We must often be willing to hear what we do not like, else we cannot prove all things. His patient attendance on their discourses he pleads, [1.] As that which entitled him to a liberty of speech in his turn and empowered him to require their attention. <hi type="italic">Hanc veniam petimusque damusque vicissim—This liberty we mutually allow and ask.</hi> Those that have heard may speak, and those that have learned may teach. [2.] As that which enabled him to pass a judgment upon what they had said. He had observed what they aimed at, and therefore knew what to say to it. Let us be thoroughly apprized of the sentiments of our brethren before we censure them; for <hi type="italic">he that answers a matter before he hears it,</hi> or when he has heard it only by halves, <hi type="italic">it is folly and shame to him,</hi> and bespeaks him both impertinent and imperious. <div eID="gen10050" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10051" type="x-p"/> II. A man of great sense and courage, and one that knew as well when and how to speak as when and how to keep silence. Though he had so much respect to his friends as not to interrupt them with his speaking, yet he had so much regard to truth and justice (his better friends) as not to betray them by his silence. He boldly pleads, <div eID="gen10051" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> 1. That man is a rational creature, and therefore that every man has for himself a judgment of discretion and ought to be allowed a liberty of speech in his turn. He means the same that Job did (<reference osisRef="Job.12.2">ch. xii. 3</reference>, <hi type="italic">But I have understanding as well as you</hi>) when he says (<reference osisRef="Job.32.8">v. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">But there is a spirit in man;</hi> only he expresses it a little more modestly, that one man has understanding as well as another, and no man can pretend to have the monopoly of reason or to engross all the trade of it. Had he meant <hi type="italic">I have revelation as well as you</hi> (as some understand it), he must have proved it; but, if he meant only <hi type="italic">I have reason as well as you,</hi> they cannot deny it, for it is every man's honour, and it is no presumption to claim it, nor could they gainsay his inference from it (<reference osisRef="Job.32.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Therefore hearken to me.</hi> Learn here, (1.) That the soul is a spirit, neither material itself nor dependent upon matter, but capable of conversing with things spiritual, which are not the objects of sense. (2.) It is an understanding spirit. It is able to discover and receive truth, to discourse and reason upon it, and to direct and rule accordingly. (3.) This understanding spirit is in every man; it is the light <hi type="italic">that lighteth every man,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.9">John i. 9</reference>. (4.) It is the inspiration of the Almighty that gives us this understanding spirit; for he is the Father of spirits and fountain of understanding. See <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen. ii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.12.7">Eccl. xii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.12.1">Zech. xii. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen10052" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10053" type="x-p"/> 2. That those who are advanced above others in grandeur and gravity do not always proportionably go beyond them in knowledge and wisdom (<reference osisRef="Job.32.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">Great men are not always wise;</hi> it is a pity but they were, for then they would never do hurt with their greatness and would do so much the more good with their wisdom. Men should be preferred for their wisdom, and those that are in honour and power have most need of wisdom and have the greatest opportunity of improving in it; and yet it does not follow that great men are always wise, and therefore it is folly to subscribe to the dictates of any with an implicit faith. The aged do not always understand judgment; even <hi type="italic">they</hi> may be mistaken, and therefore must not expect to bring every thought into obedience to them: nay, <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> they must not take it as an affront to be contradicted, but rather take it as a kindness to be instructed, by their juniors: <hi type="italic">Therefore I said, hearken to me,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.32.10">v. 10</reference>. We must be willing to hear reason from those that are every way inferior to us, and to yield to it. He that has a good eye can see further upon level ground than he that is purblind can from the top of the highest mountain. <hi type="italic">Better is a poor and wise child then an old and foolish king,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.4.13">Eccl. iv. 13</reference>. <div eID="gen10053" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> 3. That it was requisite for something to be said, for the setting of this controversy in a true light, which, by all that had hitherto been said, was but rendered more intricate and perplexed (<reference osisRef="Job.32.13">v. 13</reference>): "I must speak, <hi type="italic">lest you should say, We have found out wisdom,</hi> lest you should think your argument against Job conclusive and irrefragable, and that Job cannot be convinced and humbled by any other argument than this of yours, <hi type="italic">That God casteth him down and not man,</hi> that it appears by his extraordinary afflictions that God is his enemy, and therefore he is certainly a wicked man. I must show you that this is a false hypothesis and that Job may be convinced without maintaining it." Or, "Lest you should think you have found out the wisest way, to reason no more with him, but leave it to God to thrust him down." It is time to speak when we hear errors advanced and disputed for, especially under pretence of supporting the cause of God with them. It is time to speak when God's judgments are vouched for the patronizing of men's pride and passion and their unjust uncharitable censures of their brethren; then we must speak on God's behalf. <div eID="gen10054" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> 4. That he had something new to offer, and would endeavour to manage the dispute in a better manner than it had hitherto been managed, <reference osisRef="Job.32.14">v. 14</reference>. He thinks he may expect a favourable hearing; for, (1.) He will not reply to Job's protestations of his integrity, but allows the truth of them, and therefore does not interpose as his enemy: "<hi type="italic">He hath not directed his words against me.</hi> I have nothing to say against the main scope of his discourse, nor do I differ from his principles. I have only a gentle reproof to give him for his passionate expressions." (2.) He will not repeat their arguments, nor go upon their principles: "<hi type="italic">Neither will I answer him with your speeches</hi>—not with the same matter, for should I only say what has been said I might justly be silenced as impertinent,—nor in the same manner; I will not be guilty of that peevishness towards him myself which I dislike in you." The controversy that has already been fully handled a wise man will let alone, unless he can amend and improve what has been done; why should he <hi type="italic">actum agere—do that which has been done already?</hi>
entries.20aedbb9f515eedfb6bc1a674833d286d5b7c1de: <div eID="gen10055" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10056" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> They were amazed, they answered no more: they left off speaking. <hi type="super">16</hi> When I had waited, (for they spake not, but stood still, <hi type="italic">and</hi> answered no more;) <hi type="super">17</hi> <hi type="italic">I said,</hi> I will answer also my part, I also will show mine opinion. <hi type="super">18</hi> For I am full of matter, the spirit within me constraineth me. <hi type="super">19</hi> Behold, my belly <hi type="italic">is</hi> as wine <hi type="italic">which</hi> hath no vent; it is ready to burst like new bottles. 20 I will speak, that I may be refreshed: I will open my lips and answer. <hi type="super">21</hi> Let me not, I pray you, accept any man's person, neither let me give flattering titles unto man. <hi type="super">22</hi> For I know not to give flattering titles; <hi type="italic">in so doing</hi> my maker would soon take me away. <div eID="gen10056" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> Three things here apologize for Elihu's interposing as he does in this controversy which had already been canvassed by such acute and learned disputants:— <div eID="gen10057" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10058" type="x-p"/> 1. That the stage was clear, and he did not break in upon any of the managers on either side: <hi type="italic">They were amazed</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.32.15">v. 15</reference>); <hi type="italic">they stood still, and answered no more,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.32.16">v. 16</reference>. They not only left off speaking themselves, but they stood still, to hear if any of the company would speak their minds, so that (as we say) he had room and fair play given him. They seemed not fully satisfied themselves with what they had said, else they would have adjourned the court, and not have stood still, expecting what might further be offered. And therefore <hi type="italic">I said</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.32.17">v. 17</reference>), "<hi type="italic">I will answer also my part.</hi> I cannot pretend to give a definitive sentence; no, the judgment is the Lord's, and by him it must be determined who is in the right and who is in the wrong; but, since you have each of you shown your opinion, I also will show mine, and let it take its fate with the rest." When what is offered, even by the meanest, is offered thus modestly, it is a pity but it should be fairly heard and considered. I see no inconvenience in supposing that Elihu here discovers himself to be the penman of this book, and that he here writes as an historian, relating the matter of fact, that, after he had bespoken their attention in the foregoing verses, they were amazed, they left off whispering among themselves, did not gainsay the liberty of speech he desired, but stood still to hear what he would say, being much surprised at the admirable mixture of boldness and modesty that appeared in his preface. <div eID="gen10058" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10059" type="x-p"/> 2. That he was uneasy, and even in pain, to be delivered of his thoughts upon this matter. They must give him leave to speak, for he cannot forbear; while he is <hi type="italic">musing the fire burns</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.39.3">Ps. xxxix. 3</reference>), <hi type="italic">shut up in his bones,</hi> as the prophet speaks, <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jer. xx. 9</reference>. Never did nurse, when her breasts were gorged, so long to have them drawn as Elihu did to deliver his mind concerning Job's case, <reference osisRef="Job.32.18-Job.32.20">v. 18-20</reference>. If any of the disputants had hit that which he thought was the right joint, he would contentedly have been silent; but, when he thought they all missed it, he was eager to be trying his hand at it. He pleads, (1.) That he had a great deal to say: "<hi type="italic">I am full of matter,</hi> having carefully attended to all that has hitherto been said, and made my own reflections upon it." When aged men are drawn dry, and have spent their stock, in discoursing of the divine Providence, God can raise up others, even young men, and fill them with matter for the edifying of his church; for it is a subject that can never be exhausted, though those that speak upon it may. (2.) That he was under a necessity of saying it: "<hi type="italic">The spirit within me</hi> not only instructs me what to say, but puts me on to say it; so that if I have not vent (such a ferment are my thoughts in) I shall <hi type="italic">burst like bottles of new wine</hi> when it is working," <reference osisRef="Job.32.19">v. 19</reference>. See what a great grief it is to a good minister to be silenced and thrust into a corner; he is full of matter, full of Christ, full of heaven, and would speak of these things for the good of others, but he may not. (3.) That it would be an ease and satisfaction to himself to deliver his mind (<reference osisRef="Job.32.20">v. 20</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will speak, that I may be refreshed,</hi> not only that I may be eased of the pain of stifling my thoughts, but that I may have the pleasure of endeavouring, according to my place and capacity, to do good. It is a great refreshment to a good man to have liberty to speak for the glory of God and the edification of others. <div eID="gen10059" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10060" type="x-p"/> 3. That he was resolved to speak, with all possible freedom and sincerity, what he thought was true, not what he thought would please (<reference osisRef="Job.32.21-Job.32.22">v. 21, 22</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Let me not accept any man's person,</hi> as partial judges do, that aim to enrich themselves, not to do justice. I am resolved to flatter no man." He would not speak otherwise than he thought, either, (1.) In compassion to Job, because he was poor and in affliction, would not make his case better than he really took it to be, for fear of increasing his grief; "but, let him bear it as he can, he shall be told the truth." Those that are in affliction must not be flattered, but dealt faithfully with. When trouble is upon any it is foolish pity to suffer sin upon them too (<reference osisRef="Lev.19.17">Lev. xix. 17</reference>), for that is the worst addition that can be to their trouble. Thou shalt not countenance, any more than discountenance, <hi type="italic">a poor man in his cause</hi> (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.3">Exod. xxiii. 3</reference>), nor regard a sad look any more than a big look, so as, for the sake of it, to pervert justice, for that is accepting persons. Or, (2.) In compliment to Job's friends, because they were in prosperity and reputation. Let them not expect that he should say as they said, any further than he was convinced that they say right, nor applaud their dictates for the sake of their dignities. No, though Elihu is a young man, and upon his preferment, he will not dissemble truth to court the favour of great men. It is a good resolution he has taken up—"<hi type="italic">I know not to give flattering titles to men;</hi> I never used myself to flattering language;" and it is a good reason he gives for that resolution—<hi type="italic">in so doing my Maker would soon take me away.</hi> It is good to keep ourselves in awe with a holy fear of God's judgments. He that made us will take us away in his wrath we do not conduct ourselves as we should. He hates all dissimulation and flattery, and will soon <hi type="italic">put lying lips to silence</hi> and <hi type="italic">cut off flattering lips,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.12.3">Ps. xii. 3</reference>. The more closely we eye the majesty of God as our Maker, and the more we dread his wrath and justice, the less danger shall we be in of a sinful fearing or flattering of men.  <chapter eID="Job.32"/> <div eID="gen10060" type="x-p"/>

entries.13c7d7848358df6963cfd30f22edbb8f765af1e1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5162"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 32</title> <div sID="gen7682" type="x-p"/> Job 32:1-37:24. Speech of Elihu.<div eID="gen7682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7683" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5162"/>1-6. Prose (poetry begins with "I am young").<div eID="gen7683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7684" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">because, &c.--</hi>and because they could not prove to him that he was unrighteous. <div eID="gen7684" type="x-p"/>
entries.c4319ceb4d161455ea52b8f3d006ca7cc7aa76ee: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5167"/><div sID="gen7693" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5167"/><hi type="bold">7. Days--</hi>that is, the aged (<reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference>). <div eID="gen7693" type="x-p"/>
entries.836d2775df2900b3b7e4c28d2bd40316b1b71506: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5168"/><div sID="gen7694" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5168"/>8. Elihu claims inspiration, as a divinely commissioned messenger to Job (<reference osisRef="Job.33.6">Job 33:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.23">23</reference>); and that claim is not contradicted in <reference osisRef="Job.42.4">Job 42:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.42.5">5</reference>. Translate: "But the spirit (which God puts) in man, and the inspiration ... is that which giveth," &c.; it is not mere "years" which give understanding (<reference osisRef="Prov.2.6">Pr 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.20.22">Joh 20:22</reference>). <div eID="gen7694" type="x-p"/>
entries.8ddcdb7defd1bf477e04cb8f31a87c1255d92677: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5169"/><div sID="gen7695" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5169"/><hi type="bold">9. Great--</hi>rather, "old" (<reference osisRef="Job.32.6">Job 32:6</reference>). So Hebrew, in <reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">Ge 25:23</reference>. "Greater, less" for the older, the younger.<div eID="gen7695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7696" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">judgment--</hi>what is right. <div eID="gen7696" type="x-p"/>
entries.ab96c453c2f4db394465c6a9a7e546f786d8ee2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5170"/><div sID="gen7697" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5170"/>10. Rather, "I say."<div eID="gen7697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7698" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opinion--</hi>rather, "knowledge." <div eID="gen7698" type="x-p"/>
entries.8e20b0d2f66351f635797a7e5379b51ce770cf47: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5171"/><div sID="gen7699" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5171"/>11. Therefore Elihu was present from the first.<div eID="gen7699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7700" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reasons--</hi>literally, "understandings," that is, the meaning intended by words.<div eID="gen7700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7701" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">whilst--</hi>I waited until you should discover a suitable reply to Job. <div eID="gen7701" type="x-p"/>
entries.000697fdf0afd7cc097ce5b312673c54b5aaa8bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5172"/><div sID="gen7702" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5172"/>13. This has been so ordered, "lest you should" pride yourselves on having overcome him by your "wisdom" (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.23">Jr 9:23</reference>, the great aim of the Book of Job); and that you may see, "God alone can thrust him down," that is, confute him, "not man." So Elihu grounds his confutation, not on the maxims of sages, as the friends did, but on his special commission from God (<reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">33:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.6">6</reference>). <div eID="gen7702" type="x-p"/>
entries.3981d9b24d5173e2890f319f2f26d85339c8d6fb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5173"/><div sID="gen7703" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5173"/>14. I am altogether unprejudiced. For it is not I, whom he addressed. "Your speeches" have been influenced by irritation. <div eID="gen7703" type="x-p"/>
entries.503ed7db029148ad5407b06b5f9c025805f3c70d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5174"/><div sID="gen7704" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5174"/>15. Here Elihu turns from the friends to Job: and so passes from the second person to the third; a transition frequent in a rebuke (<reference osisRef="Job.18.3">Job 18:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.18.4">4</reference>).<div eID="gen7704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7705" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they left off--</hi>Words were taken from them. <div eID="gen7705" type="x-p"/>
entries.61bea8607b41906a0db0faeca55a11655be531f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5175"/><div sID="gen7706" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5175"/><hi type="bold">17. my part--</hi>for my part.<div eID="gen7706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7707" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">opinion--</hi>knowledge. <div eID="gen7707" type="x-p"/>
entries.f7eeef86f0ab62f253f53ff8f8a074d06bbb4f22: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5176"/><div sID="gen7708" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5176"/>18. "I am full of words," whereas the friends have not a word more to say.<div eID="gen7708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7709" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the spirit--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">33:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.20.9">Jr 20:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.18.5">Ac 18:5</reference>). <div eID="gen7709" type="x-p"/>
entries.8a40ffbcff1d124e9a0d0b0d0e93e40340baa641: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5177"/><div sID="gen7710" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5177"/><hi type="bold">19. belly--</hi>bosom: from which the words of Orientalists in speaking seem to come more than with us; they speak gutturally. "Like (new) wine (in fermentation) without a vent," to work itself off. New wine is kept in new goatskin bottles. This fittingly applies to the young Elihu, as contrasted with the old friends (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.7">Mt 9:7</reference>). <div eID="gen7710" type="x-p"/>
entries.23eb0a8e3277839cc5c29906aad4a3be82c5e1b0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5178"/><div sID="gen7711" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5178"/><hi type="bold">20. refreshed--</hi>literally, "that there may be air to me" (<reference osisRef="1Sam.16.23">1Sa 16:23</reference>). <div eID="gen7711" type="x-p"/>
entries.e3be4d748ca1cbb6b87ccb90b2c21d7f9320979a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5179"/><div sID="gen7712" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5179"/>21. "May I never accept," &c. Elihu alludes to Job's words (<reference osisRef="Job.13.8">Job 13:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.13.10">10</reference>), wherein he complains that the friends plead for God partially, "accepting His person." Elihu says he will not do so, but will act impartially between God and Job. "And I will not give flattery," &c. (<reference osisRef="Prov.24.23">Pr 24:23</reference>). <div eID="gen7712" type="x-p"/>
entries.686acaba62450506ab00207c01a84a6378d46d31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5180"/><div sID="gen7713" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5180"/><hi type="bold">22. take me away--</hi>as a punishment (<reference osisRef="Ps.102.24">Psa 102:24</reference>). <chapter eID="Job.32"/>

entries.6bc7a28bb805ed63fa8ddb25364a6284c5532406: <div eID="gen17522" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17523" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17524" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17524" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17523" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17525" type="x-p"/> Elihu comes forward, and empresses his disapprobation both of Job and his three friends - with the one for justifying himself; and with the others for taking up the subject in a wrong point of view, and not answering satisfactorily - and makes a becoming apology for himself, vv. 1-22. <div eID="gen17525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17526" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17527" type="x-p"/> These three men ceased to answer Job - They supposed that it was of no use to attempt to reason any longer with a man who justified himself before God. The truth is, they failed to convince Job of any point, because they argued from false principles; and, as we have seen, Job had the continual advantage of them. There were points on which he might have been successfully assailed; but they did not know them. Elihu, better acquainted both with human nature and the nature of the Divine law, and of God's moral government of the world, steps in, and makes the proper discriminations; acquits Job on the ground of their accusations, but condemns him for his too great self-confidence, and his trusting too much in his external righteousness; and, without duly considering his frailty and imperfections, his incautiously arraigning the providence of God of unkindness in its dealings with him. This was the point on which Job was particularly vulnerable, and which Elihu very properly clears up. <div eID="gen17527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17528" type="x-p"/> Because he was righteous tn his own eyes - The Septuagint, Syriac, Arabic, and Chaldee, all read, "Because he was righteous in Their eyes;" intimating, that they were now convinced that he was a holy man, and that they had charged him foolishly. The reading of these ancient versions is supported by a MS. of the thirteenth century, in Dr. Kennicott's collections; which, instead of בעיניו beeinaiv, in His eyes, has בעיניהם beeineyhem, in Their eyes. This is a reading of considerable importance, but it is not noticed by De Rossi. Symmachus translates nearly in the same way: Δια τον αυτον δικαιον φαινεσθαι επ' αυτων; Because he appeared more righteous than themselves.
entries.dfbdb15682701a4c490fb21a44c5a43986e21717: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17529" type="x-p"/> Then was kindled the wrath - This means no more than that Elihu was greatly excited, and felt a strong and zealous desire to vindicate the justice and providence of God, against the aspersions of Job and his friends. <div eID="gen17529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17530" type="x-p"/> Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite - Buz was the second son of Nahor, the brother of Abram, <reference osisRef="Gen.22.21">Gen 22:21</reference>. <div eID="gen17530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17531" type="x-p"/> Of the kindred of Ram - Kemuel was the third son of Nahor; and is called in Genesis (see above) the father of Aram, which is the same as Ram. A city of the name of Buz is found in <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">Jer 25:23</reference>, which probably had its name from this family; and, as it is mentioned with Dedan and Tema, we know it must have been a city in Idumea, as the others were in that district. Instead of the kindred of Ram, the Chaldee has of the kindred of Abraham. But still the question has been asked, Who was Elihu? I answer, He was "the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the kindred of Ram:" this is all we know of him. But this Scriptural answer will not satisfy those who are determined to find out mysteries where there are none. Some make him a descendant of Judah; St. Jerome, Bede, Lyranus, and some of the rabbins, make him Balaam the son of Beor, the magician; Bishop Warburton makes him Ezra the scribe; and Dr. Hodges makes him the second person in the glorious Trinity, the Lord Jesus Christ, and supposes that the chief scope of this part of the book was to convict Job of self-righteousness, and to show the necessity of the doctrine of justification by faith! When these points are proved, they should be credited. <div eID="gen17531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17532" type="x-p"/> Because he justified himself rather than God - Literally, he justified his soul, נפשו naphhso, before God. He defended, not only the whole of his conduct, but also his motives, thoughts, etc.
entries.bff1db66bbca716355be2e5f33ee2abcde5edb28: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17533" type="x-p"/> They had found no answer - They had condemned Job; and yet could not answer his arguments on the general subject, and in vindication of himself.
entries.2f052beea465dea032e2097afcc8f0325f78c39a: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17534" type="x-p"/> I am young - How young he was, or how old they were, we cannot tell; but there was no doubt a great disparity in their ages; and among the Asiatics the youth never spoke in the presence of the elders, especially on any subject of controversy.
entries.691fc6169964d2c54e06ab79608a64195e381dd6: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17535" type="x-p"/> Days should speak - That is, men are to be reputed wise and experienced in proportion to the time they have lived. The Easterns were remarkable for treasuring up wise sayings: indeed, the principal part of their boasted wisdom consisted in proverbs and maxims on different subjects.
entries.bcfeff3924d19c2b131dc60fda711869d89e754c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17536" type="x-p"/> But there is a spirit in man - Mr. Good translates: - "But surely there is an afflation in mankind, <div eID="gen17536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17537" type="x-p"/> And the inspiration of the Almighty actuateth them." <div eID="gen17537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17538" type="x-p"/> Coverdale, thus: - <div eID="gen17538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17539" type="x-p"/> Every man (no doute) hath a mynde; but it is the inspyracion of the Almightie that geveth understondinge. <div eID="gen17539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17540" type="x-p"/> I will now offer my own opinion, but first give the original text: רוח היא באנוש ונשמת שדי תבינם ruach hi beenosh venishmath shaddai tebinem. "The spirit itself is in miserable man, and the breath of the Almighty causeth them to understand," How true is it that in God we live, move, and have our being! The spirit itself is in man as the spring or fountain of his animal existence, and by the afflatus of this spirit he becomes capable of understanding and reason, and consequently of discerning Divine truth. The animal and intellectual lives are here stated to be from God; and this appears to be an allusion to man's creation, <reference osisRef="Gen.2.7">Gen 2:7</reference> : "And God breathed into man's nostrils the breath of lives," נשמת חיים nishmath chaiyim, i.e., animal and intellectual, and thus he became a living soul, נפש חיה nephesh chaiyah, a rational animal. When man fell from God, the Spirit of God was grieved, and departed from him; but was restored, as the enlightener and corrector, in virtue of the purposed incarnation and atonement of our Lord Jesus; hence, he is "the true Light that lighteth every man that cometh into the world," <reference osisRef="Joh.1.9">Joh 1:9</reference>. That afflatus is therefore still continued to אנוש enosh, man, in his wretched, fallen state; and it is by that Spirit, the רוח אלהים Ruach Elohim, "the Spirit of the merciful or covenant God," that we have any conscience, knowledge of good and evil, judgment in Divine things, and, in a word, capability of being saved. And when, through the light of that Spirit, convincing of sin, righteousness, and judgment, the sinner turns to God through Christ, and finds redemption in his blood, the remission of sins; then it is the office of that same Spirit to give him understanding of the great work that has been done in and for him; "for the Spirit itself (αυτο το Πνευμα, <reference osisRef="Rom.8.16">Rom 8:16</reference>, the same words in Greek as the Hebrew רוח היא ruach hi of Elihu) beareth witness with his spirit that he is a child of God." It is the same Spirit which sanctifies, the same Spirit that seals, and the same Spirit that lives and works in the believer, guiding him by his counsel till it leads him into glory. In this one saying, independently of the above paraphrase, Elihu spoke more sense and sound doctrine than all Job's friends did in the whole of the controversy.
entries.b40019f955d225860c39ab4ae4575f098ed55ccd: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17541" type="x-p"/> Great men are not always wise - This is a true saying, which the experience of every age and every country increasingly verifies. And it is most certain that, in the case before us, the aged did not understand judgment; they had a great many wise and good sayings, which they had collected, but showed neither wisdom nor discretion in applying them.
entries.7fdd1449a48dd14cb16459ccc2c42ba8b0fccccd: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17541" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17542" type="x-p"/> I waited for your words; I gave ear to your reasons - Instead of תבונותיכם tebunotheychem, your reasons, תכונותיכם techunotheychem, your arguments, is the reading of nine of Kennicott's and De Rossi's MSS. The sense, however, is nearly the same. <div eID="gen17542" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17543" type="x-p"/> Whilst ye searched out what to say - עד תחקרון מלין ad tachkerun millin; "Whilst ye were searching up and down for words." A fine irony, which they must have felt.
entries.8107a4dc16c6c2a40d9d9cdb6a7db795035c0795: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17543" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17544" type="x-p"/> Yea, I attended unto you - Instead of ועדיכם veadeychem, and unto you, one MS. reads the above letters with points that cause it to signify and your testimonies; which is the reading of the Syriac, Arabic, and Septuagint. <div eID="gen17544" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17545" type="x-p"/> Behold, there was none of you that convinced Job - Confuted Job. They spoke multitudes of words, but were unable to overthrow his arguments.
entries.7184f36295d9c8aaeb723910334fe78862013de8: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17545" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17546" type="x-p"/> We have found out wisdom - We by dint of our own wisdom and understanding, have found out the true system of God's providence; and have been able to account for all the sufferings and tribulations of Job. Had they been able to confute Job, they would have triumphed over him in their own self-sufficiency. <div eID="gen17546" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17547" type="x-p"/> God thrusteth him down, not man - This is no accidental thing that has happened to him: he is suffering under the just judgments of God, and therefore he must be the wicked man which we supposed him to be.
entries.96a7a842c75b9eb963263078b5305434a09cdecf: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17547" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17548" type="x-p"/> He hath not directed - I am no party in this controversy; I have no party feeling in it: he has not spoken a word against me, therefore I have no cause of irritation. I shall speak for truth; not for conquest or revenge. Neither will I answer him with your speeches; your passions have been inflamed by contradiction, and you have spoken foolishly with your lips.
entries.735d2a6408a1fa2e95aaf54fc28c570728e8650a: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17548" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17549" type="x-p"/> They were amazed - Mr. Good translates: "They (the speeches) are dissipated; they no longer produce effect; the words have flirted away from them." Your words, being without proper reference and point, are scattered into thin air: there is nothing but sound in them; they are quite destitute of sense. But I prefer the words as spoken of Job's friends. They took their several parts in the controversy as long as they could hope to maintain their ground: for a considerable time they had been able to bring nothing new; at last, weary of their own repetitions, they gave up the contest.
entries.1b0e7bc5dffe28a43cc463a4146856e661c5cc36: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17550" type="x-p"/> When I had waited - I waited to hear if they had any thing to reply to Job; and when I found them in effect speechless, then I ventured to come forward.
entries.4c16ecb272acbc2ac0196b91b5b7eaa26c8c018f: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17550" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17551" type="x-p"/> I will answer also my part - אענה חלקי aaneh chelki, "I will recite my portion." We have already seen that the book of Job is a sort of drama, in which several persons have their different parts to recite. Probably the book was used in this way, in ancient times, for the sake of public instruction. Eliphaz, Zophar, and Bildad, had recited their parts, and Job had responded to each: nothing was brought to issue. Elihu, a bystander, perceiving this, comes forward and takes a part, when all the rest had expended their materials: yet Elihu, though he spoke well, was incapable of closing the controversy; and God himself appears, and decides the case.
entries.d77e99bdb08ff74d100b22ec9d748896a9fda2fc: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17552" type="x-p"/> I am full of matter - מלים millim, "I am full of Words," or sayings; i.e., wise sentences, and ancient opinions. <div eID="gen17552" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17553" type="x-p"/> The spirit within me constraineth me - How similar to the words of St. Paul! The love of Christ constraineth us. Elihu considered himself under the influence of that Spirit of God which gives understanding, and felt anxiously concerned for the welfare both of Job and his friends.
entries.741af1f973c903ca89e685c9c6ed53221920ba18: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen17553" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17554" type="x-p"/> My belly is as wine which hath no vent - New wine in a state of effervescence. <div eID="gen17554" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17555" type="x-p"/> Like new bottles - Bottles, or rather bags, made of goat-skins. The head and shanks being cut off, the animal is cased out of the skin. The skin is then properly dressed; the anus and four shank holes properly tied up; and an aperture left at the neck or in some other place for the liquor to be poured in, and drawn out. One of these now lies before me, well tanned, and beautifully ornamented, and capable of holding many gallons. They are used, not only to carry wine and water, but for butter, and also for various dry goods. I have mentioned this in another place. When the wine is in a state of fermentation, and the skin has no vent, these bottles or bags are ready to burst; and if they be old, the new wine destroys them, breaks the old stitching, or rends the old skin. Our Lord makes use of the same figure, <reference osisRef="Mat.9.17">Mat 9:17</reference> (note); where see the note.
entries.498333030b580f97fa7aaedf7af56f4348aeef2a: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17555" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17556" type="x-p"/> I will open my lips and answer - In the preceding verse Elihu compares himself to a skin-bottle, in which the wine was in a state of fermentation, and the bottle ready to burst for want of vent. He carries on the metaphor in this verse: the bottle must be opened to save it from bursting; I will Open my mouth.
entries.f37e61eba1ea995eb61459a0d1183e8dfe1a3772: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17556" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17557" type="x-p"/> Let me not - accept any man's person - I will speak the truth without fear or favor. <div eID="gen17557" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17558" type="x-p"/> Neither let me give flattering titles - I will not give epithets to any man that are not descriptive of his true state. I will not beguile him by telling him he is what he is not. אכנה acanneh, from כנה canah, is generally supposed to signify to surname, to put a name to or upon a name, as the French word surnom implies. It means to give proud titles to persons who are worthless. It is well known that the Arabs make court to their superiors by carefully avoiding to address them by their proper names, instead of which they salute them with some title or epithet expressive of respect - Scott See below. Titles expressive of office, ecclesiastical, civil, or military, are always proper, and never forbidden, because they serve for distinction; but the Asiatic titles are in general bombastically and sinfully complimentary. The reader will find several specimens at the end of this chapter.
entries.33cad6449d68e124c706d2d7a8791758e3fc979c: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17558" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17559" type="x-p"/> My Maker would soon take me away - Were I to copy this conduct while under the influence which I now feel, God might justly consume me as in a moment. He is my Maker; he made me to know truth, to tell truth, and to live according to truth; for he is the God of truth: I shall, therefore through his help, speak the Truth, the Whole Truth, and Nothing but the Truth. <div eID="gen17559" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17560" type="x-p"/> We find from the above that vain titles of ceremony, expressive of the most eminent qualities, were given to worthless men, from time immemorial; and no wonder, for hypocrisy entered into man at the same time that sin entered into the world. <div eID="gen17560" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17561" type="x-p"/> Of the flattering titles used in the East, I shall give a few specimens from the (Arabic) Kooayid us Sultanet Shah Jehan, or, "The Rules observed during the Reign of the Mogul Emperor Shah Jehan." <div eID="gen17561" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17562" type="x-p"/> Speaking of the emperor, he is entitled, "The Sun which illuminates the firmament in the universe of royalty and dominion; the Moon, which irradiates the sky of monarchy and felicity; the King who in pomp resembles Gem-sheed. His hand is boundless as the ocean in bestowing bounties, being the key of the gates of kindness and liberality!" Again: - "The Sun of the heaven of prosperity and empire, the Shadow of God, the Asylum of the Universe, the splendor of whose instructive front causes light and gladness to the world and to mankind." "The just and vigilant Monarch; the Asylum of Truth, the Refuge of the World; the Diffuser of Light, the Solver of all human difficulties." "The Lord of the Age, who is endowed with such perfect excellence, both in internal and external qualifications, that on all occasions he holds fast the thread of good counsel, prudence, and purity of morals." "The faculty of apprehension is possessed by him in such a degree, that before the matter ha s scarcely obtained utterance he comprehends the purport, and gives answers with the tongue of inspiration." <div eID="gen17562" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17563" type="x-p"/> Addresses to Persons of Distinction "Let them convey to the presence of glorious empire, the Sultan, in pomp like Solomon, the center of the universe, powerful as heaven!" "Let them who kiss the carpet of the palace, in pomp like heaven, convey this letter to his majesty, whose sight is as creative as alchymy, king of kings, the asylum of the world!" "To the exalted presence, which gratifies the desires of all people, the most beneficent of the age, the vizier, protector of the universe, may the Almighty perpetuate his fortune!" "May this letter be dignified in the presence of Naweeb Saheb, diffuser of benefits, of exalted pomp, the respectable, the discriminator of ranks! May his power increase!" "Let them convey this to the perusal of his excellency, conversant in realities and mysteries, the support of excellencies, the cream of his contemporaries, and the cherisher of the poor!" <div eID="gen17563" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17564" type="x-p"/> These are a specimen of the flattering titles given in the East to persons in eminent stations. Their kings they clothe in all the attributes of the Deity, when both in their public and private character they are corrupt and unholy, rascals in grain, and the ruthless oppressors of suffering humanity.  <chapter eID="Job.32"/> <div eID="gen17564" type="x-p"/>

entries.dcdb6f3cd1e65ad454b9fccdd865d9186e4c9dae: <reference osisRef="Job.32.1-Job.3.1">Job 32:1-3 1</reference>-<reference osisRef="Job.3.3">3</reference>  So these three men ceased to answer Job, because he was righteous in his own eyes. And the wrath of Elihu, the son of Barachel the Buzite, of the family of Ram, was kindled: against Job was his wrath kindled, because he justified himself at the expense of God. And against his three friends was his wrath kindled, because they found no answer, and condemned Job. <div eID="gen8320" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8321" type="x-p"/> The name of the speaker is אליהוּא (with <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>), son of בּרכאל (with <hi type="italic">Munach</hi>) the buwziy (with <hi type="italic">Zarka</hi>). The name <hi type="italic">Elihu</hi> signifies “my God is He,” and occurs also as an Israelitish name, although it is not specifically Israelitish, like <hi type="italic">Elijah</hi> (my God is Jehovah). <hi type="italic">Bârach'el</hi> (for which the mode of writing בּרכאל with <hi type="italic">Dag. implic.</hi> is also found) signifies “may God bless!” (Olsh. §277, S. 618); for proper names, as the Arabian grammarians observe, can be formed both into the form of assertory clauses (<hi type="italic">ichbâr</hi>), and also into the form of modal (<hi type="italic">inshâ</hi>); the name ברכאל is in this respect distinguished from the specifically Israelitish name בּרכיה (Jehovah blesseth). The accompanying national name defines the scene; for on the one side בּוּז and עוּץ, according to <reference osisRef="Gen.22.21">Gen 22:21</reference>, are the sons of Nahor, Abraham’s brother, who removed with him (though not at the same time) from Ur Casdim to Haran, therefore by family Aramaeans; on the other side, בּוּז, <reference osisRef="Jer.25.23">Jer 25:23</reference>, appears as an Arab race, belonging to the קצוּצי פאה (comp. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.25">Jer 9:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.32">Jer 49:32</reference>), i.e., to the Arabs proper, who cut the hair of their heads short all round (περιτρόχαλα, Herodotus iii. 8), because wearing it long was accounted as disgraceful (vid., Tebrâzi in the <hi type="italic">Hamâsa</hi>, p. 459, l. 10ff.). Within the Buzite race, Elihu sprang from the family of רם. Since רם is the name of the family, not the race, it cannot be equivalent to ארם (like רמּים,   <reference osisRef="2Chr.22.5">2Ch 22:5</reference>, = ארמים), and it is therefore useless to derive the Aramaic colouring of Elihu’s speeches from design on the part of the poet. But by making him a Buzite, he certainly appears to make him an Aramaean Arab, as Aristeas in Euseb. <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. ix. 25 calls him Ἐλιοῦν τὸν Βαραξηιὴλ τὸν Ζωβίτην (from ארם צובה). It is remarkable that Elihu’s origin is given so exactly, while the three are described only according to their country, without any statement of father or family. It would indeed be possible, as Lightfoot and Rosenm. suppose, for the poet to conceal his own name in that of Elihu, or to make allusion to it; but an instance of this later custom of Oriental poets is found nowhere else in Old Testament literature. <div eID="gen8321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8322" type="x-p"/> The three friends are silenced, because all their attempts to move Job to a penitent confession that his affliction is the punishment of his sins, have rebounded against this fact, that he was righteous in his own eyes, i.e., that he imagined himself righteous; and because they now (שׁבת of persons, in distinction from חדל, has the secondary notion of involuntariness) know of nothing more to say. Then Elihu’s indignation breaks forth in two directions. First, concerning Job, that he justified himself מאלהים, i.e., not <hi type="italic">a Deo</hi> (so that He would be obliged to account him righteous, as <reference osisRef="Job.4.17">Job 4:17</reference>), but <hi type="italic">prae Deo.</hi> Elihu rightly does not find it censurable in Job, that as a more commonly self-righteous man he in general does not consider himself a sinner, which the three insinuate of him (<reference osisRef="Job.15.14">Job 15:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.25.4">Job 25:4</reference>), but that, declaring himself to be righteous, he brings upon God the appearance of injustice, or, as Jehovah also says further on, <reference osisRef="Job.40.8">Job 40:8</reference>, that he condemns God in order that he may be able to maintain his own righteousness. Secondly, concerning the three, that they have found no answer by which they might have been able to disarm Job in his maintenance of his own righteousness at the expense of the divine justice, and that in consequence of this they have condemned Job. Hahn translates: so that they should have represented Job as guilty; but that they have not succeeded in stamping the servant of God as a רשׁע, would wrongly excite Elihu’s displeasure. And Ewald translates: and that they had nevertheless condemned him (§345, <hi type="italic">a</hi>); but even this was not the real main defect of their opposition. The <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> describes the condemnation as the result of their inability to hit upon the right answer; it was a miserable expedient to which they had recourse. According to the Jewish view, ויּרשׁיעוּ את־איּוב is one of the eighteen תקוני סופרים (<hi type="italic">correctiones scribarum</hi>), since it should be וירשׁיעו את־האלהים. But it is not the friends who have been guilty of this sin of הרשׁיע against God, but Job, <reference osisRef="Job.40.8">Job 40:8</reference>, to whom Elihu opposes the sentence אל לא־ירשׁיע, Job 34:12. Our judgment of another such <hi type="italic">tiqqûn</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>, was more favourable. That Elihu, notwithstanding the inward conviction to the contrary by which he is followed during the course of the controversial dialogue, now speaks for the first time, is explained by what follows.
entries.630a0f472db060a8e06e1d3483273508eb76182a: <reference osisRef="Job.32.4-Job.5.4">Job 32:4-5 4</reference>-<reference osisRef="Job.5.6">6</reference> And Elihu had waited for Job with words, for they were older than he in days. And Elihu saw that there was no answer in the mouth of the three men, then his wrath was kindled. And Elihu the son of Barachel the Buzite began, and said. <div eID="gen8322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8323" type="x-p"/> He had waited (<hi type="italic">perf.</hi> in the sense of the <hi type="italic">plusquamperf.,</hi> Ew. §135, <hi type="italic">a</hi>) for Job with words (בּדברים as elsewhere בּמלּים, בּמלּין), i.e., until Job should have spoken his last word in the controversial dialogue. Thus he considered it becoming on his part, for they (המּה, <hi type="italic">illi,</hi> whereas אלּה according to the usage of the language is <hi type="italic">hi</hi>) were older (<hi type="italic">seniores</hi>) than he in days (לימים as <reference osisRef="Job.32.6">Job 32:6</reference>, less harsh here, instead of the <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of closer definition, <reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.11.9">Job 11:9</reference>). As it now became manifest that the friends made no reply to Job’s last speeches for want of the right solution of problem, and therefore also Job had nothing further to say, he believes that he may venture, without any seeming want of courtesy, to give utterance to his long-restrained indignation; and Elihu (with <hi type="italic">Mahpach</hi>) the son of Barach'el (<hi type="italic">Mercha</hi>) the Buzite (with <hi type="italic">Rebia parvum</hi>) began and spoke (ויּאמר not with <hi type="italic">Silluk</hi>, but <hi type="italic">Mercha mahpach.,</hi> and in fact with <hi type="italic">Mercha</hi> on the accented <hi type="italic">penult.,</hi> as <reference osisRef="Job.3.2">Job 3:2</reference>, and further).
entries.d780f44a052f8cebd5dfe7b0d26aaa9a9aeca7b0: <reference osisRef="Job.32.6-Job.7.6">Job 32:6-7   6</reference> <hi type="italic">b</hi> I am young in days, and ye are hoary, <div eID="gen8323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8324" type="x-p"/> Therefore I stood back and was afraid <div eID="gen8324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8325" type="x-p"/> To show you my knowledge.   7  I thought: Let age speak, <div eID="gen8325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8326" type="x-p"/> And the multitude of years teach wisdom. <div eID="gen8326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8327" type="x-p"/> It becomes manifest even here that the Elihu section has in part a peculiar usage of the language. זחל in the signification of Arab. <hi type="italic">zḥl</hi>, cogn. with Arab. <hi type="italic">dḥl</hi>, דּחל, to frighten back;<note placement="foot">The lexicographers explain the Arab. <hi type="italic">zḥl</hi> by <hi type="italic">zâla</hi> (זול), to stand away from, back, to retreat, or <hi type="italic">tanahha</hi>, to step aside; <hi type="italic">Piel, Hiph.,</hi> to push any one aside, place anything back; <hi type="italic">Hithpa.,</hi> to keep one’s self on one side; adj. זחל, זחיל, זחוּל, etc., standing back. Thus the town of <hi type="italic">Zahla</hi> in the plain of the Lebanon takes its name from the fact that it does not stand out in the plain, but is built close at the foot of the mountain in a corner, and consequently retreats. And <hi type="italic">zuhale</hi> (according to the <hi type="italic">Kamus</hi>) is an animal that creeps backwards into its hole, e.g., the scorpion; and hence, improperly, a man who, as we say with a similar figure, never comes out of his hole, always keeps in his hole, i.e., never leaves his dwelling, as <hi type="italic">zuhal</hi> in general signifies a man who retires or keeps far from active life; in connection with which also the planet Saturn is called <hi type="italic">Zuhal</hi>, the retreating one, on account of its great distance from the rest. Slippery (of ground) is זחלוּל, because it draws the foot backwards (<hi type="italic">muzhil</hi>) by its smoothness, and thus causes the walker to fall. A further formation is זחלק, to be slippery, and to slip in a slippery place; beside which, זלק, a word of similar meaning, is no longer used in Syria. According to this Arabic primary notion of <hi type="italic">zḥl</hi>, it appears זחלי ארץ, Mic 7:17, is intended to describe the serpents not as creeping upon the earth, but as creeping into the earth (comp. the name of the serpent, <hi type="italic">achbi' at el - ard ,</hi> those that hide themselves in the earth); but in Talmud. and Aram. זחל used of animals has the general signification to creep, and of water, to <hi type="italic">glide</hi> (flow gently down). The primary notion, to glide (to slip, creep, flow gently, <hi type="italic">labi</hi>), is combined both in the derivatives of the root זח and in those of the root זל with the notion of a departing and retreating motion. - Wetzst. and Fl.</note> and דּע for דּעת (here and <reference osisRef="Job.32.10">Job 32:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.32.17">Job 32:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.3">Job 36:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference>) occurs nowhere else in the Old Testament; על־כּן (comp. לכן, <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>) is used only by Elihu within the book of Job. ימים, days = fulness of days, is equivalent to advanced age, old age with its rich experience. רב with its plural genitive is followed (as כל sa( d usually is) by the predicate in the <hi type="italic">plur.;</hi> it is the attraction already described by מספר, <reference osisRef="Job.15.10">Job 15:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.21">Job 21:21</reference>, Ges. §148, 1.
entries.62fd7a0b7efb0d83ed9083049f19288179c4ea26: <reference osisRef="Job.32.8-Job.10.8">Job 32:8-10   8</reference>  Still the spirit, it is in mortal man, <div eID="gen8327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8328" type="x-p"/> And the breath of the Almighty, that giveth them understanding.   9  Not the great in years are wise, <div eID="gen8328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8329" type="x-p"/> And the aged do not understand what is right. 10  Therefore I say: O hearken to me, <div eID="gen8329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8330" type="x-p"/> I will declare my knowledge, even I. <div eID="gen8330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8331" type="x-p"/> The originally affirmative and then (like אוּלם) adversative אכן also does not occur elsewhere in the book of Job. In contradiction to biblical psychology, Rosenm. and others take <reference osisRef="Job.32.8">Job 32:8</reference> as antithetical: Certainly there is spirit in man, but ... . The two halves of the verse are, on the contrary, a synonymous (“the spirit, it is in man, viz., that is and acts”) or progressive parallelism) thus according to the accents: ”the spirit, even that which is in man, and ... ”). It is the Spirit of God to which man owes his life as a living being, according to <reference osisRef="Job.33.4">Job 33:4</reference>; the spirit of man is the principle of life creatively wrought, and indeed breathed into him, by the Spirit of God; so that with regard to the author it can be just as much God’s רוּח or נשׁמה, <reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job 34:14</reference>, as in respect of the possessor: man’s רוח or נשׁמה. All man’s life, his thinking as well as his bodily life, is effected by this inwrought principle of life which he bears within him, and all true understanding, without being confined to any special age of life, comes solely from this divinely originated and divinely living spirit, so far as he acts according to his divine origin and basis of life. רבּים are here (as the opposite of צעירים, <reference osisRef="Gen.25.23">Gen 25:23</reference>) <hi type="italic">grandes</hi> = <hi type="italic">grandaevi</hi> (lxx πολυχρόνιοι). לא governs both members of the verse, as <reference osisRef="Job.3.10">Job 3:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.28.17">Job 28:17</reference>; Job 30:24. Understanding or ability to form a judgment is not limited to old age, but only by our allowing the πνεῦμα to rule in us in its connection with the divine. Elihu begs a favourable hearing for that of which he is conscious. דּע, and the Hebr.-Aramaic הוּה, which likewise belong to his favourite words, recur here.
entries.8464df9b3a650c67bfde51be6bcb920fc7a8c7b5: <reference osisRef="Job.32.11-Job.14.11">Job 32:11-14 11</reference>  Behold, I waited upon your words, <div eID="gen8331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8332" type="x-p"/> Hearkened to your perceptions, <div eID="gen8332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8333" type="x-p"/> While ye searched out replies. 12  And I attended closely to you, <div eID="gen8333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8334" type="x-p"/> Yet behold: there was no one who refuted Job, <div eID="gen8334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8335" type="x-p"/> Who answered his sentences, from you. 13  Lest ye should say: “We found wisdom, <div eID="gen8335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8336" type="x-p"/> God is able to smite him, not man!” 14  Now he hath not arranged his words against me, <div eID="gen8336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8337" type="x-p"/> And with your sentences I will not reply to him. <div eID="gen8337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8338" type="x-p"/> He has waited for their words, viz., that they might give utterance to such words as should tend to refute and silence Job. In what follows, עד still more emphatically than ל refers this aim to that to which Elihu had paid great attention: I hearkened to your understandings, i.e., explanations of the matter, that, or whether, they came forth, (I hearkened) to see if you searched or found out words, i.e., appropriate words. Such abbreviated forms as אזין = אאזין (comp. מזין = מיזין for מעזין, <reference osisRef="Prov.17.4">Pro 17:4</reference>, Ges. §68, rem. 1, if it does not signify <hi type="italic">nutriens</hi>, from זוּן) we shall frequently meet with in this Elihu section. In <reference osisRef="Job.32.12">Job 32:12</reference>, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.32.12">Job 32:12</reference></hi> evidently is related as an antecedent to what follows: and I paid attention to you (עדיכם contrary to the analogy of the cognate <hi type="italic">praep</hi>. instead of עדיכם, moreover for עליכם, with the accompanying notion: intently, or, according to Aben-Duran: thoroughly, without allowing a word to escape me), and behold, intently as I paid attention: no one came forward to refute Job; there was no one from or among you who answered (met successfully) his assertions. Every unbiassed reader will have an impression of the remarkable expressions and constructions here, similar to that which one has in passing from the book of the Kings to the characteristic sections of the Chronicles. The three, Elihu goes on to say, shall not indeed think that in Job a wisdom has opposed them - a false wisdom, indeed - which only God and not any man can drive out of the field (נדף, Arab. <hi type="italic">ndf , discutere, dispellere,</hi> as the wind drives away chaff or dry leaves); while he has not, however (ולא followed directly by a <hi type="italic">v. fin.</hi> forming a subordinate clause, as <reference osisRef="Job.42.3">Job 42:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.44.18">Psa 44:18</reference>, and freq., Ew. §341, <hi type="italic">a</hi>), arrayed (ערך in a military sense, <reference osisRef="Job.33.5">Job 33:5</reference>; or forensic, <reference osisRef="Job.23.4">Job 23:4</reference>; or even as <reference osisRef="Job.37.19">Job 37:19</reference>, in the general sense of <hi type="italic">proponere</hi>) words against him (Elihu), i.e., utterances before which he would be compelled to confess himself affected and overcome. He will not then also answer him with such opinions as those so frequently repeated by them, i.e., he will take a totally different course from theirs in order to refute him.
entries.a9ef1d936790c75d6d47fc14049bf63937569047: <reference osisRef="Job.32.15-Job.17.15">Job 32:15-17 15</reference>  They are amazed, they answer no more, <div eID="gen8338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8339" type="x-p"/> Words have fled from them. 16  And I waited, for they spake not, <div eID="gen8339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8340" type="x-p"/> For they stand still, they answer no more. 17  Therefore I also will answer for my part, <div eID="gen8340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8341" type="x-p"/> I will declare my knowledge, even I. <div eID="gen8341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8342" type="x-p"/> In order to give a more rapid movement and an emotional force to the speech, the figure asyndeton is introduced in <reference osisRef="Job.32.15">Job 32:15</reference>, as perhaps in <reference osisRef="Jer.15.7">Jer 15:7</reference>, Ew. §349, <hi type="italic">a</hi>. Most expositors render העתּיקוּ passively, according to the sense: they have removed from them, i.e., are removed from them; but why may העתיק not signify, like <reference osisRef="Gen.12.8">Gen 12:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.26.22">Gen 26:22</reference>, to move away, viz., the tent = to wander on (Schlottm.)? The figure: words are moved away (as it were according to an encampment broken up) from them, i.e., as we say: they have left them, is quite in accordance with the figurative style of this section. It is unnecessary to take והוחלתּי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.32.16">Job 32:16</reference></hi>, with Ew. (§342, <hi type="italic">c</hi>) 2 and Hirz. as <hi type="italic">perf. consec</hi>. and interrogative: and should I wait, because they speak no more? Certainly the interrog. part. sometimes disappears after the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of consequence, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.13">Eze 18:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.24">Eze 18:24</reference> (and will he live?); but by what would והוחלתי be distinguished as <hi type="italic">perf. consec.</hi> here? Hahn’s interpretation: I have waited, until they do not speak, for they stand ... , also does not commend itself; the poet would have expressed this by עד לא ידברו, while the two כי, especially with the poet’s predilection for repetition, appear to be co-ordinate. Elihu means to say that he has waited a long time, surprised that the three did not speak further, and that they stand still without speaking again. Therefore he thinks the time is come for him also to answer Job. אענה cannot be <hi type="italic">fut. Kal,</hi> since where the 1 <hi type="italic">fut. Kal</hi> and <hi type="italic">Hiph.</hi> cannot be distinguished by the vowel within the word (as in the <hi type="italic">Ayin Awa</hi> and double <hi type="italic">Ayin</hi> verbs), the former has an inalienable <hi type="italic">Segol;</hi> it is therefore 1 <hi type="italic">fut. Hiph.,</hi> but not as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">Ecc 5:19</reference> in the signification to employ labour upon anything (lxx περισπᾶν), but in an intensive <hi type="italic">Kal</hi> signification (as הזעיק for זעק, <reference osisRef="Job.35.9">Job 35:9</reference>, comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.31.18">Job 31:18</reference>): to answer, to give any one an answer when called upon. Ewald’s supposedly proverbial: I also plough my field! (§192, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, Anm. 2) does unnecessary violence to the usage of the language, which is unacquainted with this הענה, to plough. It is perfectly consistent with Elihu’s diction, that חלקי beside אני as permutative signifies, “I, my part,” although it might also be an <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of closer definition (as <hi type="italic">pro parte mea,</hi> for my part), or even - which is, however, less probable - <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of the obj. (my part). Elihu speaks more in the scholastic tone of controversy than the three.
